newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: FEATURE - Former Namibian guerrillas protest for jobs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Former Namibian guerrillas protest for jobs.

text.p: Seven years ago Namibia won its independence from South Africa and the party which led the liberation struggle took power.

The South West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO) is still in power, but members of its armed wing which spearheaded the military campaign are unable to make a living and say they have been abandoned.
"We were in exile fighting for liberation, but when we came back home there were no jobs for us," said Ndapanda Amukwaya.

She is one of 3,000 ex-members of the People's Liberation Army of Namibia (PLAN) and the pre-independence South West Africa Territory Force (SWATF) who say they should not be in the ranks of the unemployed.
Around 60 percent of Namibia's 1.5 million people are estimated to be without formal employment.

A peaceful transition to independence took place under a U.N.-sponsored plan linked to the withdrawal of Cuban troops from neighbouring Angola and elections saw SWAPO take power on independence day, March 21, 1990.
President Sam Nujoma inherited many problems, including high unemployment, from the South African administrators who ruled the country then known as South West Africa for 75 years.
OLD FIGHTERS STILL WAIT FOR BETTER LIFE
The former fighters say they want jobs and better lives promised by Nujoma and SWAPO during the 23-year struggle for independence.
"We need jobs, permanent jobs," said Amukwaya, a member of a committee representing the former combatants.
Among those who have joined the protests to demand employment are Namibians who worked with South Africa's "Koevoet" (crowbar) counter-intelligence police unit which operated in the country.
PLAN had an estimated 15,000 combatants, while the former SWATF and Koevoet fighters numbered up to 8,000.
During the recent demonstrations, more than 300 former fighters occupied the gardens at the president's State House in Windhoek demanding to see Nujoma.
They later moved to the capital's showgrounds and their numbers swelled to over 2,000.

"We wanted to see the comrade president himself," Amukwaya said. "He was leading us in exile...and he is the one who knows the way we are suffering. All of us suffered for the past seven years. All of us should get jobs."
PROTESTS SPUR ACTION FROM NUJOMA
Nujoma called an emergency cabinet meeting on the matter, and the ministers came up with a promise of over 4,000 jobs.
Of these 1,000 are with the special field force of the Namibian police and 2,000 with Patriotic Construction, a work brigade company which also does training.
Nearly 400 jobs have been promised in the ministries of works, transport and communications and 740 in the ministry of environment and tourism.
Several private companies have also offered to help.
"We believe the president, but we are still registering ourselves and then we will go back home and wait for the day of employment," Amukwaya said.
Theopoline Ashipala, now 29, left her motherland in 1980.
"I was 12 when I left for Angola. At 17 I became a combatant and now I am suffering," she said.
"I've been looking for a job, but people in Namibia do not want to recruit ex-fighters because we don't have certificates for studies."

A 35-year-old man who did not want to be named, said: "I want to learn and I want to show my children that I can also do something. I am very glad that finally we will get a job, it doesn't matter what type to me."

While former PLAN fighters have begun registering for the promised jobs, the union representing old SWATF fighters was planning a separate protest on July 11 to demand that the Namibian government pay them the compensation wages awarded by South Africa during 1991/92, which they say they have not received.

Under the compensation scheme, South Africa made a one-off payment of 12,000 Namibian dollars ($2,600) to former Koevoet and SWATF fighters as a gratuity to tide them over until they found employment. The Namibian and Pretoria governments say the money was disbursed.
